headline: Drumcree dispute: PSNI says 'major public safety operation' to continue

Ireland PoliticsDrumcree: Major public safety operation under way as NI Secretary appeals for calmImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said the PSNI is doing everything it can to maintain order and ensure the safety of everyone in that area

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has said a "major public safety operation" will continue in Portadown this weekend.

The PSNI is "continuing to seek safe and peaceful compliance with the Parades Commission determination" at Drumcree and said its "investigation into anyone suspected of breaking the law related to this dispute is continuing at pace".

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant urged calm and said "everyone across Northern Ireland wants a peaceful resolution to the situation".

On Wednesday, the PSNI chief constable said there would be an investigation after protesters blocked the mainly nationalist road to prevent an Orange Order parade from happening.

Image source, PA MediaImage caption, DUP leader Gavin Robinson said there has to be "consequences" to "people who are law makers who are acting as law breakers"

Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said the PSNI was doing "everything we can to maintain order and ensure the safety of everyone in that area".

"I want to thank those officers from Police Services in England and Scotland who have been in Northern Ireland supporting our efforts over the past week," he added.

"Finally, I want to repeat the Chief Constable's appeal for calm and for all parties to refocus efforts on working to find a lasting resolution to this issue."

Protesters remain on Garvaghy Road and the Orange Order has maintained a presence at Drumcree church after talks to end the parading dispute ended without agreement.

Sir Chris Bryant said on social media he was "continuing to work to find a mutually acceptable agreement and I'm grateful to everyone who has offered help and has taken part in the discussions so far".

"My door remains open and I repeat my calls for people to support further compromise," he added.

"I would also encourage people to ignore calls for more people to come to the area at this time of tension."

Meanwhile just after 22:00 BST on Friday, Portadown Orangemen made another attempt to parade down the Garvaghy Road.

As has been the case with repeated attempts this week, a senior PSNI officer stopped them at the bottom of Drumcree Hill.

Earlier on Friday, the Orange Order's Portadown District said that its position "has been clear from the outset: we set out to complete our parade through lawful and peaceful means, and despite the provocation and threats we have faced, it remains our firm intention to continue on that path".

"Our community has demonstrated considerable restraint, dignity and patience, and we strongly encourage everyone to continue conducting themselves lawfully and peacefully," it added in a social media post, external.

It said "rounds of talks with the Secretary of State concluded last night without agreement" and the "District is now carefully assessing the position and considering its next steps over the coming days".

The statement added that it remains "committed to pursuing a lawful and peaceful resolution".

The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said he expects the criminal investigation into the unlawful blocking of Garvaghy Road to begin next week.

Earlier, Robinson said there had to be "consequences" for "people who are law makers who are acting as law breakers".

First Minister Michelle O'Neill was among those who attended the protest. She has said she understands the law, but chose to "stand in solidarity" with residents.

Robinson said he expected the investigation to begin next week "but it needs the space to see it conclude as well".

Image caption, Orange Order members again walked to police lines at Drumcree on Friday night, but were stopped from going towards the Garvaghy Road

The fallout over the proposed Orange Order march - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning.

A fresh legal bid by the residents to prevent the march was due to be heard on Friday - but has now been postponed until Monday.

Orangemen and Garvaghy Road residents met Sir Chris Bryant at Hillsborough Castle on Thursday night but did not break their deadlock.

Speaking after Thursday night's talks, Sir Chris told reporters: "I think this is the end of these conversations.

"We haven't come to a settled agreement and it's a shame but my door remains open."

Breándan Mac Cionnaith, the chairman of the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, said there had been no "meeting of minds".

Nigel Dawson, the Orange Order's Portadown district master, said it "remains as it has been".

Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Sir Chris Bryant says he is open to hosting further talks

On Friday morning, about 20 protesters were gathered on the Garvaghy Road.

About a mile away at Drumcree Church, five members of the Orange Order were present.

The rector of Drumcree Church has said that he has received hundreds of "extremely nasty" emails, texts and calls in recent days.

In a post on Facebook, the Reverend Gary Galway said: "Social media has given a platform for individuals to express themselves without restraint, or the integrity of a face-to-face civil discussion."

Image source, PA MediaAnalysis: Momentum lost after failed talksHopes of a resolution to the Drumcree dispute have faded but have not disappeared completely.

By engaging in a four-day talks process, the two sides have shown a willingness to try to negotiate an agreement.

Further discussions at some stage are still possible. Some might say they are inevitable.

However, momentum has been lost and the danger is that the problem now just festers for days, months or even years.

That would be bad for community relations and a strain on police resources as they keep a round-the-clock watch on Drumcree hill and the Garvaghy Road.

For all concerned, a difficult road lies ahead.

The stalemate has reopened what was once the most bitter parading dispute in Northern Ireland, with stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission, which adjudicates on marching disputes, ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision that was upheld for the past 28 years.

But last week the Parades Commission decided that the parade could go ahead on Sunday morning with restrictions in place.

That prompted a large protest on the Garvaghy Road, preventing the Orange Order from marching.

Thirteen councillors have been reported to the local government standards watchdog over conduct surrounding the parading dispute.

Some 25 allegations have been received by the Local Government Commissioner for Standards in Northern Ireland in recent days concerning potential breaches of the councillors' code of conduct.

It follows unionist parties accusing nationalist politicians of acting unlawfully over their involvement in the protest at Garvaghy Road on Sunday.

On Friday, former US diplomat Dr Richard Haass told BBC News NI that Northern Ireland had "failed" to come to terms with the legacy of its past.

Haass chaired all-party talks in Northern Ireland in 2013 aimed at resolving contentious issues, including parades.

He said the flare-up of the Drumcree dispute should be "a bit of a warning shot or a wake-up call".

"I don't think any of us should take progress for granted. Backsliding is always possible," he added.

Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Orangemen gathered at Drumcree Church on Sunday but were blocked from completing their march

More than 200 people from a Protestant background have put their names to a letter to the UK and Irish governments, expressing concern over the dispute.

In the letter, they said they were distressed by the "trauma that is being visited on the residents of the Garvaghy Road after 28 years of calm".

The signatories said they recognised that parading was a "valued tradition" for many but they appealed to the Orange Order to "look towards the bigger picture and bring this impasse to an end in the interests of the entire community".
